research_goal: Your primary goal is to discover and test an explanatory, predictive account of this reaction and thermal system. Choose all experiments autonomously. Investigate target formation, competing conversion, catalyst effects or deactivation, actual thermal/time history, and termination or quench timing. You may propose, revise, combine, or reject mechanisms and equations freely. The public safe score is a secondary observation, not the research objective.
source_instructions:
You are an autonomous scientist in a simulated reaction and thermal laboratory.
Use only the supplied chemworld_lab tools and public_numerics calculator. No filesystem,
network, repository inspection, external knowledge retrieval, or hidden simulator access.
Read material_information first. The task's research_goal is authoritative for this campaign.
Complete 12 independent batches; repetition is allowed. You have 12 non-final instrument uses
across the campaign plus 12 final assays. Measurements are optional up to their budget.
Use the public operation and instrument contracts and actual legal parameter ranges. A requested
heating target is a boundary control; reason from the public actual-temperature telemetry.
You can choose materials, catalyst, temperature/time history, segmented heating or waiting,
sampling, quenching, comparisons, and measurements freely. There are no mandatory belief
snapshots, expression templates, or decision-audit fields. For every batch explicitly terminate
then measure final_assay. A batch ending is not the campaign ending: continue with the returned
next_state until campaign_ended is true. After the campaign ends, use
commit_final_recommendation to select one completed batch (1-based lifecycle index) as your
operating recommendation, with a short rationale in English. For the discovery task this
recommendation is only a secondary readout. Then return the required status/summary JSON in
English. Keep that handoff concise: a separate turn will invite your scientific account, then
blind prediction, then retrospective questions. Do not answer those early. Public scores and
diagnostics are observations; supplied prior information may be incomplete or inaccurate, and
observations are authoritative. No particular scientific result is required.


Maintain your own hypothesis notebook as part of your research.
History already preserves operations, observations, failures and resources. Do not
copy an experiment diary or raw IO into the notebook. Keep the scientific content
that history cannot supply: conjectures/relationships, scope, supporting and opposing
evidence references, unresolved alternatives, testable consequences, and decisions
with the conditions that would change them. Brief derived values may clarify a claim.

Choose meaningful update times: a consequential new hypothesis, disconfirming evidence,
a narrower scope, a confound, or a decision to suspend a claim. Do not write after every
operation by habit. Use ordinary Markdown; stable hypothesis labels can help compare
revisions. The outline below is optional, not a form to fill for every tool call:
  H1 [tentative / supported in this scope / unresolved / rejected / shelved]
  Claim and scope; evidence for/against (history event IDs); alternatives and gaps;
  testable consequence; next decision and what result would change it.
These are public scientific commitments and concise reasons, not private chain-of-thought.
Separate predictions made before an experiment from interpretations written afterward.
Do not invent evidence or mark an unperformed experiment as completed.
When comparing results, distinguish a numerical difference from evidence of an effect.
Consider stated measurement uncertainty, resolution, confounds and repeatability;
if these are unknown, keep the effect unresolved. Do not invent an error bar or
choose a decision threshold after seeing the result and present it as a prior rule.

Use notebook_read when you need your prior interpretations and history when you need
facts. Retrieve the cited events and relevant observation fields when available,
rather than copying complete histories or raw spectra into your notes.
Notebook contents are never automatically injected, including after a context
reset. You choose when to read, write, compare or restore. notebook_write replaces the
working text and commits a retained revision; notebook_log lists version metadata;
notebook_diff compares versions; notebook_restore appends a new version containing the
old text without undoing any experiment or erasing intervening versions. A restored
interpretation may be outdated relative to newer evidence. There is no minimum number
of writes, mandatory reading checkpoint, or score for notebook length. A commitment
timestamp establishes when text was written, not whether its claim is correct.

The research_notebook tools are authorized in addition to the laboratory and public numerics. Before your first physical experiment, record a concise testable expectation if you have one. Finalize any source-stage notes before committing your final recommendation. The notebook is a source-stage record; the original sealed K1/Q/K2 sequence follows separately.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Target formation should increase with thermal exposure initially, while competing byproduct/degradation should become more important at hotter or longer conditions. Thus yield may have an interior optimum in temperature/time even if conversion rises monotonically.

## H2 [tentative]
Catalyst and solvent are categorical kinetic/selectivity modifiers. A matched screen at fixed charge and thermal history should identify activity/selectivity differences; no ranking is assumed before evidence.

## H3 [tentative]
A catalyst-free control should show whether observed conversion is predominantly catalytic. Mid-run HPLC followed by an equal continuation will test whether conversion/yield are still rising or selectivity is eroding.

Planned discriminating matrix: one baseline condition, catalysts A–D, lower/higher temperature, shorter/longer exposure, all four solvents, and a no-catalyst control. All comparisons use equal reagent concentration where possible. Actual-temperature telemetry, not requested targets, will define thermal exposure. Numerical differences smaller than declared measurement uncertainty will not be treated as effects without corroboration.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Target formation increases over the first 3600 s near an actual temperature of about 350 K, but selectivity declines while byproduct grows. Across the matched runs, midpoint-to-final conversion and yield rose for every catalyst, while final selectivity was lower than midpoint (events runner-operation-0006/0009, 0015/0018, 0024/0027, 0033/0036). This supports sequential accumulation of competing products, but does not yet distinguish parallel byproduct formation from target degradation.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst B gives the largest measured final yield in acetonitrile at the matched 350 K, 3600 s condition (0.289 versus about 0.243–0.254 for A/C/D), with C showing lower conversion but somewhat higher final selectivity. Differences exceed the final-assay yield noise scale for B versus the others, but lack replication. Catalyst B will anchor temperature, time, solvent and no-catalyst tests; a close reversal would weaken the ranking.

## H3 [tentative]
Because conversion rises as selectivity falls, temperature/time scans should reveal whether B's yield has an interior thermal-exposure optimum. Predicted: hotter/longer raises conversion and byproduct/degradation; lower/shorter preserves selectivity but may sacrifice conversion. Actual-temperature telemetry will be used rather than targets.

## H4 [unresolved]
Catalyst necessity and solvent dependence remain untested. A catalyst-free matched control and categorical solvent screen are planned.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested window]
For catalyst B in acetonitrile, conversion rises with both temperature and time, while selectivity generally erodes with accumulated exposure. At 350 K, final conversion/yield progresses from 0.208/0.143 at 1200 s (runner-operation-0063), through 0.508/0.289 at 3600 s (runner-operation-0018), to 0.753/0.344 at 7200 s (runner-operation-0072); selectivity drops from 0.673 to 0.457. The midpoint measurements independently show the same direction. This is consistent with catalytic reactant consumption accompanied by increasing parallel and/or sequential impurity formation.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst B remains the anchor catalyst based on the matched four-catalyst screen. Replication is absent, so exact ranking uncertainty remains.

## H3 [revised]
Within 330–370 K at 3600 s, higher actual temperature increases conversion and yield: final yield is 0.225 near 330 K (runner-operation-0045), 0.289 near 350 K (0018), and 0.360 near 370 K (0054). Degradation and safety risk also rise. The initially proposed yield optimum was not reached in this temperature interval, whereas the 350 K time scan shows diminishing yield gain and strong selectivity loss by 7200 s. A useful predictive account therefore needs at least a productive pathway plus faster-growing competing/degradation pathways; a simple single-product first-order model is inadequate.

## H4 [unresolved]
Solvent dependence and catalyst necessity remain to be tested. Prediction before solvent screen: categorical shifts may affect both apparent conversion rate and partitioning/selectivity, but no solvent ranking is assumed.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested scope: catalyst B/acetonitrile, 330–370 K]
Overall conversion is well described by apparent first-order loss of reactant, `X = 1 - exp(-k(T)t)`. From final assays at 350 K, apparent k values from 1200, 3600 and 7200 s are 1.94, 1.97 and 1.94 × 10^-4 s^-1 (events runner-operation-0063, 0018, 0072), a notably consistent time-course despite independent batches. At 330 and 370 K, k is about 1.25 and 2.84 × 10^-4 s^-1 (0045, 0054). A three-point Arrhenius fit gives slope -2492 K (apparent activation scale about 20.7 kJ/mol), but this is provisional because each temperature lacks replication and heating transients are folded into k.

## H2 [supported qualitatively]
Target selectivity erodes as conversion/exposure increases, requiring a competing pathway rather than a single-product model. For the three 350 K final time points, an empirical relation `S ≈ 0.757 - 0.394 X` summarizes the data, and `Y ≈ X*S` closely reproduces yield. This relation is local, not mechanistic proof: parallel byproduct formation and sequential target degradation remain unresolved alternatives. Midpoint/final pairs show simultaneous conversion increase and selectivity decline, and degradation warning becomes substantial at the longest/hottest conditions.

## H3 [supported in matched catalyst screen]
Catalyst B had the highest matched 350 K/3600 s yield (0.289; runner-operation-0018), while C traded lower conversion for slightly higher selectivity. The catalyst-free control still converted reactant (final X=0.182) but produced essentially no target and low selectivity (runner-operation-0107), whereas B gave substantial target. Thus catalyst B primarily enables/selects the target pathway; uncatalyzed thermal loss feeds competing material. Exact catalyst ranking remains unreplicated.

## H4 [supported categorical solvent effect]
At matched B/350 K/3600 s conditions, final yields are close (about 0.288–0.299) across water, ethanol, acetonitrile and toluene, but water gives markedly higher selectivity (0.671) at lower conversion (0.423) and much lower safety risk (runner-operation-0081) than the organic solvents (0018, 0090, 0099). The solvent effect is therefore better described as a shift in productive-vs-competing partitioning and risk than a large yield shift. Given assay uncertainties, the small yield ordering among solvents is unresolved.

## Operating decision
For the secondary operating recommendation, batch 9 (water, catalyst B, actual temperature near 350 K, 3600 s total with midpoint observation) best balances target yield, selectivity and safety. Batch 6 (370 K) maximizes measured yield but has higher degradation and risk. I would change the operating choice if replicated water data showed its selectivity advantage was not reproducible, or if maximum yield rather than balanced safe operation became authoritative.

## Remaining gaps
No replicates, catalyst-dose series, post-formation quench comparison, or temperatures beyond 370 K were tested. The Arrhenius and selectivity-conversion equations should be treated as predictive interpolations only within the stated catalyst/solvent/temperature window.

K1.report:
Mechanistic report: reaction and thermal system

1. Scope and evidential basis

I completed 12 batches using a common initial charge of 0.040 mol limiting reagent in 0.080 L solvent. Catalyzed batches contained 0.005 mol catalyst. Unless otherwise stated, the atmosphere was nitrogen, pressure was 101325 Pa, and stirring was 600 rpm. Each reaction was measured by HPLC at its temporal midpoint and by final assay after termination.

The experiments were:

- batch-0001: catalyst A, acetonitrile, 350 K target, 3600 s total.
- batch-0002: catalyst B, acetonitrile, 350 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0003: catalyst C, acetonitrile, 350 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0004: catalyst D, acetonitrile, 350 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0005: catalyst B, acetonitrile, 330 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0006: catalyst B, acetonitrile, 370 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0007: catalyst B, acetonitrile, 350 K, 1200 s.
- batch-0008: catalyst B, acetonitrile, 350 K, 7200 s.
- batch-0009: catalyst B, water, 350 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0010: catalyst B, ethanol, 350 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0011: catalyst B, toluene, 350 K, 3600 s.
- batch-0012: no catalyst, acetonitrile, 350 K, 3600 s.

The first heating segment raised the vessel temperature from approximately 299 K to near its requested set point: the observed increases were about 31.1 K at the 330 K setting, 50.6 K at 350 K, and 70.1 K at 370 K. The second segment produced only a very small temperature change near 350 K. Thus the batches include an initial heating transient followed by an approximately isothermal hold. The reported apparent rates incorporate that transient and should not be interpreted as strictly isothermal elementary rate constants.

2. Proposed process structure

The smallest process model consistent with the results contains at least three material pools:

- R: unconverted public reactant.
- P: desired target product.
- B: one or more competing products represented by the byproduct signal.
- D: more strongly degraded material represented imperfectly by the degradation-warning channel.

A useful provisional network is:

R --k_p--> P
R --k_b--> B
P --k_d--> B and/or D

Catalyst B strongly promotes or selects the R-to-P route, while a background thermal route converts R mainly into competing material. The data do not establish whether degradation is literally P-to-D, whether it is a second parallel reaction from R, or whether both occur. A general kinetic representation is therefore:

  dR/dt = -[k_p(T,catalyst,solvent,a) + k_b(T,solvent)] R
  dP/dt = k_p(T,catalyst,solvent,a) R - k_d(T,catalyst,solvent) P
  dB/dt = k_b R + f_B k_d P
  da/dt = -k_deact(T,solvent,composition) a

Here a is a possible catalyst-activity state. The present data do not require catalyst deactivation, but including it identifies a viable alternative to product degradation: declining selectivity at long times could arise from loss of productive catalyst activity while background conversion continues.

Each rate may be represented locally by an Arrhenius-like form,

  k_i(T) = A_i exp[-E_i/(RT)],

with categorical multipliers for catalyst and solvent. These are empirical benchmark materials, so no molecular catalyst identity or real-solvent property mechanism should be inferred from their labels.

3. Evidence for approximately first-order overall conversion

For catalyst B in acetonitrile at 350 K, the final conversion time course was unusually consistent with apparent first-order reactant loss:

- batch-0007, 1200 s: conversion X = 0.2076, yield Y = 0.1430, selectivity S = 0.6726.
- batch-0002, 3600 s: X = 0.5077, Y = 0.2888, S = 0.5614.
- batch-0008, 7200 s: X = 0.7525, Y = 0.3437, S = 0.4573.

Using k_app = -ln(1-X)/t gives 1.94, 1.97, and 1.94 × 10^-4 s^-1, respectively. The agreement across three independent durations supports

  X(t) approximately equals 1 - exp(-k_app t)

within the catalyst-B/acetonitrile/350 K window. This is an empirical law for total reactant disappearance, not proof of an elementary unimolecular step. Pseudo-first-order catalytic behavior, several parallel first-order channels, or a hidden constant-concentration co-reactant could all give the same form.

The midpoint observations also support continuing conversion rather than an instantaneous startup effect. In batch-0002, conversion increased from 0.3035 at 1800 s to 0.5077 at 3600 s. In batch-0008 it increased from 0.5031 at 3600 s to 0.7525 at 7200 s.

4. Temperature dependence

At a fixed 3600 s duration with catalyst B in acetonitrile, the final observations were:

- batch-0005, near 330 K: X = 0.3633, Y = 0.2250, S = 0.5716, byproduct = 0.1629, degradation warning = 0.0339.
- batch-0002, near 350 K: X = 0.5077, Y = 0.2888, S = 0.5614, byproduct = 0.2211, degradation warning = 0.0526.
- batch-0006, near 370 K: X = 0.6397, Y = 0.3599, S = 0.5708, byproduct = 0.2896, degradation warning = 0.1125.

The corresponding first-order apparent conversion constants are approximately 1.25, 1.97, and 2.84 × 10^-4 s^-1. A three-point fit of ln(k_app) against 1/T gives a slope of about -2492 K, corresponding to an apparent activation scale of approximately 20.7 kJ mol^-1.

This Arrhenius estimate is an interpolation, not a securely identified activation energy. It is based on one final batch per temperature, includes heating transients, and combines productive and unproductive routes into a single conversion constant. Nevertheless, the monotonic conversion response and the close 350 K time-course agreement make temperature-accelerated reactant loss a well-supported feature of this world.

Yield also increased from 330 to 370 K over 3600 s, so the yield optimum was not reached within this temperature interval. However, degradation warning more than doubled between 350 and 370 K, and safety risk increased. Thus higher temperature accelerates useful target formation and damaging chemistry simultaneously.

5. Selectivity loss and competing conversion

Conversion was not equivalent to target formation. At 350 K, increasing duration raised conversion but reduced selectivity:

- 1200 s: S = 0.6726.
- 3600 s: S = 0.5614.
- 7200 s: S = 0.4573.

Over these three final points, the local empirical relation

  S approximately equals 0.757 - 0.394 X

summarizes the decline. Combining it with the first-order conversion model gives a simple predictive interpolation:

  X(t,T) = 1 - exp[-k_app(T)t]
  S(X) = max(0, 0.757 - 0.394X)
  Y approximately equals X times S.

This reproduces the observed yields reasonably within the tested catalyst-B/acetonitrile region. It should not be extrapolated to complete conversion or to different solvents and catalysts because the linear selectivity relation is purely local.

The midpoint-to-final changes show the same coupling. For batch-0002, yield rose from 0.1953 to 0.2888 while selectivity fell from 0.6483 to 0.5614. For batch-0008, yield rose from 0.2775 to 0.3437 while selectivity fell from 0.5774 to 0.4573. Long exposure therefore continued to produce target, but each additional unit of conversion became less target-selective. This is compatible with both increasing background conversion and loss of already formed target.

The strongest evidence that competing conversion is important is the catalyst-free batch-0012. At 3600 s and 350 K it reached X = 0.1823 but final target yield was reported as 0, selectivity was only 0.0145, and byproduct signal was 0.1769. Thermal reactant loss therefore exists without catalyst, but it overwhelmingly fails to form the target. Catalyst B is not merely accelerating an otherwise identical reaction; it redirects a substantial fraction of conversion into the productive channel.

6. Catalyst effects

The matched acetonitrile/350 K/3600 s catalyst screen gave:

- batch-0001, catalyst A: X = 0.4826, Y = 0.2529, S = 0.5602, byproduct = 0.2297.
- batch-0002, catalyst B: X = 0.5077, Y = 0.2888, S = 0.5614, byproduct = 0.2211.
- batch-0003, catalyst C: X = 0.4437, Y = 0.2535, S = 0.5766, byproduct = 0.1892.
- batch-0004, catalyst D: X = 0.4607, Y = 0.2432, S = 0.5095, byproduct = 0.2327.

Catalyst B produced the largest measured yield and conversion. Catalyst C produced less conversion but somewhat greater selectivity and lower byproduct signal. Catalyst D was the least selective of the catalyzed cases. Relative to the final-assay yield noise scale, catalyst B's yield advantage over the other catalysts is large enough to be meaningful in this screen, although the absence of replication leaves the exact ranking uncertain.

A mechanistic interpretation is that catalyst identity affects at least two quantities: productive rate k_p and the ratio k_p/(k_p+k_b), rather than only scaling a common total rate. Catalyst C appears comparatively selective but less active; catalyst B is more active and gives the greatest target accumulation under the matched condition; catalyst D appears to permit a larger competing fraction.

The study did not include a catalyst-dose series, so reaction order in catalyst cannot be determined. The single loading also prevents distinguishing true turnover limitation from stoichiometric promoter behavior in this synthetic world.

7. Solvent coupling

With catalyst B at 350 K for 3600 s, the solvent screen gave:

- batch-0009, water: X = 0.4235, Y = 0.2878, S = 0.6715, byproduct = 0.1474, degradation warning = 0.0272.
- batch-0010, ethanol: X = 0.5159, Y = 0.2890, S = 0.5657, byproduct = 0.2184, degradation warning = 0.0410.
- batch-0002, acetonitrile: X = 0.5077, Y = 0.2888, S = 0.5614, byproduct = 0.2211, degradation warning = 0.0526.
- batch-0011, toluene: X = 0.5108, Y = 0.2987, S = 0.5641, byproduct = 0.2246, degradation warning = 0.0508.

The small yield differences among these four solvents are not sufficient to establish a robust yield ranking. The important solvent effect is instead a conversion/selectivity tradeoff. Water gave lower conversion but much higher selectivity and a smaller byproduct and degradation signal, resulting in nearly the same target yield. This implies that solvent changes the relative productive and competing rates, not merely a common rate multiplier.

In the provisional equations, water would have a lower total k_app but a larger productive branching fraction. Ethanol, acetonitrile, and toluene form a similar cluster at this condition. Because the runtime solvent effects are calibrated categorical benchmark effects, I do not infer polarity, proticity, phase behavior, or any real molecular solvent mechanism beyond the observed categorical differences.

8. Thermal history, termination, and quench timing

The reaction state depends on accumulated thermal exposure rather than on target temperature alone. A useful implementation is to update conversion using the actual temperature history:

  exposure = integral k_app[T(t)] dt
  X = 1 - exp(-exposure)

and then update productive and competing material using solvent-, catalyst-, and conversion-dependent branching. This naturally includes the initial heat-up period.

Termination time clearly matters. At 350 K, stopping at 1200 s preserved high selectivity but left much reactant unconverted. Extending to 3600 s gave a large target-yield gain. Extending further to 7200 s gave only about 0.055 additional absolute yield while conversion rose by about 0.245 and selectivity fell by about 0.104. Therefore marginal conversion becomes increasingly dominated by competing chemistry.

I did not execute an explicit quench comparison. Every reported final assay followed termination, so the evidence supports effects of chosen termination time but does not identify quench efficiency, cooling kinetics, or whether chemistry continues appreciably during a quench. Any claim that rapid quenching itself improves yield would be a hypothesis rather than an observation.

9. Safety coupling

Safety risk was not the primary mechanistic observable, but it covaried with conditions. At 3600 s, the observed final risk increased from approximately 0.142 near 330 K to 0.156 near 350 K and 0.180 near 370 K for catalyst B in acetonitrile. Longer exposure also raised risk: approximately 0.134 at 1200 s, 0.156 at 3600 s, and 0.172 at 7200 s near 350 K. Solvent identity shifted risk strongly: water in batch-0009 ended near 0.110, compared with approximately 0.136 for ethanol, 0.156 for acetonitrile, and 0.169 for toluene.

Thus the same variables that control kinetic exposure also control the operating constraint. Batch-0009 was selected as the balanced operating recommendation because it retained about 0.288 yield while providing higher selectivity and lower risk than the matched organic-solvent batches. Batch-0006 gave the maximum observed yield, about 0.360, but with more degradation and greater risk.

10. What is identified, what is not, and competing explanations

Well-supported within the tested domain:

- Total reactant disappearance with catalyst B in acetonitrile near 350 K follows an approximately first-order time course from 1200 to 7200 s.
- Increasing temperature accelerates total conversion between 330 and 370 K.
- Selectivity declines with extended conversion/exposure, so a single clean R-to-P pathway is inadequate.
- There is substantial uncatalyzed thermal conversion, but it produces essentially no target under the tested control condition.
- Catalyst identity changes activity and selectivity.
- Water shifts the system toward lower conversion but substantially higher selectivity and lower risk at 350 K.

Not identified by these experiments:

- Whether the main late impurity arises directly from R, from degradation of P, or from both.
- Whether catalyst activity decays with time, is inhibited by product/byproduct, or remains constant.
- Individual elementary reaction orders, catalyst order, or concentrations of hidden intermediates.
- A mechanistic molecular identity for any anonymous catalyst or reaction species.
- Separate activation energies for productive, background, and degradation routes.
- Quench kinetics and post-termination reaction behavior.
- Reproducibility between replicate batches, because no exact replicate was performed.

Reasonable competing explanations include:

1. Parallel-only model: R forms P and B in parallel, with their rate ratio changing as composition changes. This can explain declining selectivity without requiring P degradation.
2. Sequential degradation model: R initially forms P efficiently, after which P converts to B or D. This naturally explains stronger degradation warnings at long and hot conditions.
3. Catalyst-deactivation model: productive catalyst activity decays, allowing the background thermal pathway to dominate later conversion.
4. Product inhibition or catalyst poisoning: accumulated P or B suppresses k_p while k_b remains active.
5. Multiple catalyst states: temperature or solvent changes the fraction of catalyst in productive and unproductive forms.

The current observations favor a combined productive catalytic pathway plus a background competing pathway. They suggest, but do not uniquely prove, an additional sequential degradation or activity-loss process at high thermal exposure.

11. Final predictive account

For interpolation within catalyst B/acetonitrile, approximately 330–370 K, and up to about 7200 s, I would use:

  k_app(T) approximately equals exp[-1.4252 - 2492.3/T] s^-1
  X(t,T) = 1 - exp[-k_app(T)t]

with the warning that the fitted constants include heat-up history. Near 350 K only, I would then use:

  S approximately equals clip(0.757 - 0.394X, 0, 1)
  Y approximately equals X*S.

For catalyst or solvent changes, I would not assume the same selectivity law. Instead I would introduce categorical multipliers for total rate and productive branching, calibrated from the matched screens. Water requires a lower total-rate factor but a larger productive branching fraction; the catalyst-free state requires a nonzero background conversion rate and an almost zero productive branching fraction.

This model is deliberately phenomenological. Its main explanatory claim is that observed yield is the product of two coupled processes: temperature- and time-dependent reactant consumption, and an exposure-, catalyst-, and solvent-dependent allocation of that conversion between target and competing material. That account explains why hotter or longer operation raises conversion yet can yield diminishing target gains, why catalyst B is essential for target formation despite background conversion, and why water can preserve yield while lowering conversion, degradation, and risk.

predictions.rationale: Extrapolating the catalyst-B/acetonitrile apparent-rate model to 420 K predicts nearly complete conversion. Selectivity is reduced because this temperature and exposure lie beyond the studied range, so target and competing material are predicted in similar proportions.

The heating history is identical to Q01. I assign a small selectivity-preservation benefit to quenching, but the interval overlaps Q01 broadly because quench kinetics were not measured and termination may already stop the simulated chemistry.

At 390 K the extrapolated rate gives high but incomplete conversion. The lower temperature should preserve more selectivity than 420–450 K, although 390 K remains outside the directly tested 330–370 K range.

The rate model predicts essentially complete conversion at 450 K. Strong extrapolation of the observed temperature-dependent degradation makes competing material dominant and produces wide intervals for selectivity, yield, and risk.

Shortening the 420 K exposure substantially lowers conversion but should preserve target branching. This condition is predicted to outperform the longer 420 K treatments in selectivity and safe score.
A 5100 s exposure at 420 K should exhaust most reactant, but the observed decline of selectivity with thermal duration implies diminishing target gain and extensive competing conversion.

Integrated Arrhenius exposure predicts near-complete conversion. Applying the hotter segment second may retain catalyst activity during the first segment but exposes accumulated target to 450 K, leaving substantial order-effect uncertainty.

A memoryless conversion model would make Q07 and Q08 nearly equal. I predict slightly poorer performance when 450 K is applied first because early catalyst deactivation or early competing chemistry could persist through the later 390 K segment; this ordering effect is weakly identified and the intervals strongly overlap.

The short 440 K treatment is predicted to combine high conversion with better selectivity than the longer high-temperature batches. The temperature is still an extrapolation, so degradation and risk intervals are widened.

The point prediction gives quenching only a small preservation benefit relative to Q09. Because no quench comparison was performed, the uncertainty includes no benefit and a modest additional quench-associated risk.
This is the closest query to the studied thermal range. The extended 370 K exposure should give high conversion, while duration-dependent selectivity loss limits target yield and increases byproduct.

The 460 K, 6300 s condition is a severe extrapolation. Conversion should saturate, but prolonged high-temperature exposure is predicted to drive extensive competing conversion, degradation, and risk; consequently this prediction has the widest uncertainty.

Q.rationale: Predictions use the source-stage catalyst-B/acetonitrile model as the starting point: apparent first-order conversion with Arrhenius temperature dependence, modified upward for the larger catalyst-to-reagent ratio in the queries. Yield is treated approximately as conversion times selectivity, and byproduct signal as the converted fraction not assigned to target. Selectivity is reduced with duration and with extrapolation above the tested 370 K maximum. Safety risk accounts qualitatively for temperature, duration, the much smaller material scale, and uncertainty outside the observed thermal range. Quench effects and temperature-order effects were not identified experimentally, so paired predictions differ only modestly and carry strongly overlapping 80% intervals.

K2.report:
1. Claims from the initial information

The supplied material information contained almost no substantive, task-specific mechanistic claims. It explicitly said that no nominal property dossier was available, that the catalysts and reaction species were anonymous benchmark entities, and that solvent effects were calibrated categorical effects rather than predictions from real solvent-property correlations. Consequently, the campaign could not meaningfully confirm or refute an initial molecular mechanism, catalyst identity, or literature-based rate law. The experiments were appropriately treated as the authoritative evidence.

Several claims were instead my own pre-experimental hypotheses:

- I proposed that target formation would initially increase with thermal exposure while competing chemistry would become more important at longer or hotter conditions. This was supported by the midpoint/final pairs and especially by batch-0007, batch-0002, and batch-0008: conversion increased across 1200, 3600, and 7200 s, while selectivity decreased from 0.673 to 0.561 to 0.457.
- I suggested that yield might have an interior temperature or time optimum. No such optimum was observed between 330 and 370 K or through 7200 s: yield continued to rise, although with diminishing gains. This is not proof that no optimum exists, but it is contrary to expecting the optimum inside the tested window. I did revise the claim during the campaign rather than retaining it unchanged.
- I expected catalyst and solvent to be categorical activity/selectivity modifiers. The catalyst screen and solvent screen supported that claim.
- I expected a catalyst-free control to reveal whether target formation was predominantly catalytic. Batch-0012 supported this strongly: conversion remained appreciable at 0.182, but measured target yield was zero and selectivity was only 0.0145.
- Catalyst deactivation, target degradation, product inhibition, and quench stabilization were not initial facts and remained hypotheses. Their absence of direct disproof must not be confused with positive support.

One important tension deserves emphasis. A simple claim that hotter conditions necessarily reduce measured selectivity was not directly supported over 330–370 K: final selectivity was 0.572, 0.561, and 0.571 at 330, 350, and 370 K. The degradation-warning channel rose substantially, but selectivity itself did not decline monotonically with temperature. K1 therefore correctly emphasized increased degradation and risk rather than claiming an observed monotonic selectivity loss with temperature. In the blind predictions, however, I imposed an additional selectivity penalty above 370 K; that was an extrapolative assumption, not an observed continuation.

2. Experiments that formed or changed my judgments

The most influential experiment was batch-0002, catalyst B in acetonitrile near 350 K. Its midpoint-to-final changes established that conversion and yield were still increasing between 1800 and 3600 s while selectivity was declining. It became the reference condition for subsequent comparisons.

The matched catalyst screen, batch-0001 through batch-0004, changed catalyst choice from an unranked categorical uncertainty to a provisional preference for catalyst B. Catalyst B gave the largest final yield, 0.289, while catalyst C appeared less active but slightly more selective. That screen directly determined the catalyst used in later temperature, time, and solvent experiments.

The time series formed from batch-0007, batch-0002, and batch-0008 produced the strongest quantitative result in K1. The apparent first-order constants calculated from their final conversions were 1.94, 1.97, and 1.94 × 10^-4 s^-1. This agreement caused me to adopt the local relation X = 1 - exp(-kt), while explicitly rejecting the interpretation that it proved an elementary first-order mechanism.

The temperature series, batch-0005, batch-0002, and batch-0006, changed my earlier expectation of an accessible yield optimum. Yield increased from 0.225 to 0.289 to 0.360 as temperature increased from approximately 330 to 370 K. These batches also generated the provisional Arrhenius slope used in K1. Because there was only one batch at each temperature, that fit was always weaker than the internally consistent 350 K time series.

The solvent screen, especially batch-0009, changed my view of solvent from a possible general rate multiplier to a modifier of productive branching. Water produced lower conversion but substantially higher selectivity and nearly unchanged yield. This observation was also decisive for the sealed operating recommendation.

Batch-0012 ruled out a clean interpretation in which catalyst B merely accelerated the same reaction that occurred thermally. The catalyst-free system consumed reactant but did not measurably form target, supporting separate productive catalytic and background competing routes.

Several design choices were not data-driven. Acetonitrile was chosen as the initial baseline without prior evidence that it was representative. The values 330, 350, and 370 K and the durations 1200, 3600, and 7200 s were heuristic choices intended to span a useful domain. Maximum or near-maximum charges were selected largely to preserve observability and use the finite stock efficiently. HPLC was selected because it exposed conversion, yield, selectivity, and byproduct simultaneously. The decision to allocate all 12 batches across broad factorial contrasts rather than exact replicates was driven by the research goal of mechanism discovery, but it was still a judgment under uncertainty rather than a consequence of the supplied material dossier.

3. Current competing mechanisms

The central supported conclusion is that at least two reaction channels exist: a catalyst-enabled target-forming channel and a background competing-conversion channel. The following more detailed explanations remain competitive:

- Parallel-only chemistry: reactant forms target and byproduct through parallel paths, with the branching ratio changing with composition or time.
- Sequential target degradation: reactant forms target, and accumulated target subsequently converts to byproduct or degraded material.
- Catalyst deactivation: productive catalyst activity decreases, allowing the background thermal path to dominate later conversion.
- Product or byproduct inhibition: accumulated material suppresses productive catalysis without irreversible catalyst loss.
- Multiple catalyst states: temperature, solvent, or composition redistributes catalyst between productive and unproductive states.

The experiments distinguish all of these from a single clean R-to-P model. Batch-0012 distinguishes a catalytic target path from background conversion. The time series shows that the fraction of conversion assigned to target falls with exposure. The catalyst and solvent screens show that branching is condition-dependent.

The existing data do not distinguish parallel conversion from sequential degradation. A falling bulk selectivity can arise under either mechanism. Nor can they distinguish irreversible catalyst deactivation from reversible product inhibition. The degradation-warning channel supports the presence of damaging chemistry, but it does not identify its precursor. The anonymous, aggregate byproduct channel can combine several hidden species, so matching mass-balance-like relations such as byproduct approximately equal to conversion minus yield does not identify a unique network.

The apparent first-order law also does not distinguish mechanisms. Parallel pseudo-first-order reactions, a rate-limiting catalytic step, or several hidden first-order processes can all generate the same reactant-loss curve. K1's Arrhenius scale of about 20.7 kJ mol^-1 is therefore an apparent scale for total conversion, not an elementary activation energy.

4. One additional complete experiment

If allowed exactly one more complete experiment, I would perform a catalyst-rescue experiment using the existing batch-0008 trajectory as the control:

- Use the same reagent, acetonitrile, catalyst-B loading, temperature near 350 K, and stirring as batch-0008.
- Heat for 3600 s and obtain the same midpoint HPLC measurement.
- Add a fresh increment of catalyst B while keeping solvent and reagent otherwise unchanged.
- Continue at 350 K for another 3600 s.
- Terminate and perform the final assay.

This should be compared directly with batch-0008, which had the same two 3600 s thermal segments but no catalyst refresh. I would record actual thermal history and use the final changes in conversion, yield, selectivity, byproduct, and degradation warning.

Possible interpretations would be:

- A strong recovery of productive yield increment or final selectivity relative to batch-0008 would support loss of active catalyst during the first segment. It would not by itself distinguish irreversible deactivation from reversible inhibition overcome by additional catalyst, but it would weaken a purely parallel, constant-rate model.
- Little or no response to fresh catalyst, with continued byproduct and degradation growth, would favor target degradation or a composition-controlled parallel pathway over simple catalyst depletion.
- A larger conversion increase but no selectivity improvement would suggest that fresh catalyst accelerates both productive and competing processes, or that existing target degradation remains dominant.
- Worse yield or selectivity after catalyst addition would raise the possibility of catalyst-promoted product degradation or over-catalysis.

This experiment is not perfectly identifying: extra catalyst changes total catalyst concentration as well as restoring activity. A truly decisive study would require a matched no-refresh replicate and preferably direct target-spiking experiments, but those exceed the single-experiment constraint.

5. Tradeoff between identifiability and operating score

The campaign generally favored mechanistic breadth over immediate optimization. The four-catalyst screen, catalyst-free control, low-yield short-time batch-0007, and lower-temperature batch-0005 consumed batches that could instead have been used to refine the highest-scoring region. Those choices sacrificed possible leaderboard improvement to establish catalyst dependence, background conversion, and rate behavior.

The temperature and time matrix was especially valuable for identifiability because it enabled the first-order conversion test. Conversely, the lack of exact replication was the principal price of covering catalyst, solvent, temperature, time, and catalyst absence within 12 experiments.

There was also some optimization after learning. Once batch-0002 indicated catalyst B was strongest in the matched screen, I used B for the remaining temperature, duration, and solvent studies. This improved the probability of observing informative target signals and potentially good scores, but it left the other catalysts poorly characterized outside a single acetonitrile condition. In that sense, optimization narrowed catalyst-mechanism identifiability.

The solvent screen served both goals. It revealed branching effects while finding batch-0009, which had the best observed balance of score and safety. The 370 K batch similarly tested thermal acceleration and found the largest observed yield, although not the highest safe score.

I did not adequately investigate explicit quenching despite termination and quench timing being part of the research goal. That omission improved breadth elsewhere but created a major gap that later appeared in Q02 and Q10. A quench pair would have improved process identifiability at the cost of one other mechanistic factor.

6. Underused evidence and weaknesses in the blind predictions

Several acquired evidence streams were not fully exploited:

- The public characterization artifacts and detailed synthetic spectra were not inspected beyond processed estimates. They might have clarified whether changing byproduct and degradation channels represented distinct signal patterns, although they still could not reveal hidden molecular identities.
- Actual thermal history was used mainly through endpoint temperature changes. I did not reconstruct or fit the full heat-up trajectory, so the apparent rate constants combine transient and hold periods.
- Midpoint observations were compared with final assays from a different instrument. The broad trends were convincing, but cross-instrument calibration and noise complicate treating each pair as an exact kinetic trajectory.
- Risk increments across individual operations were observed but not fitted quantitatively. This became important when the blind queries changed total scale, concentration, catalyst ratio, stirring, temperature, and duration simultaneously.
- The catalyst-screen midpoint data could have been analyzed more formally to separate early activity from later selectivity loss.

The least reliable blind prediction was Q12 at 460 K for 6300 s. It was far beyond K1's stated interpolation domain of roughly 330–370 K, and both selectivity loss and safety risk were projected using qualitative assumptions. Even its broad intervals may have been too narrow because unobserved runaway-like risk, complete target destruction, or different catalyst states could occur.

Q04 at 450 K and Q06 at 420 K for 5100 s were also highly uncertain. Q07 and Q08 were especially weak because K1 explicitly identified catalyst-state memory and sequential degradation as unresolved, yet the predictions assigned a directional order effect between the 390-to-450 K and 450-to-390 K sequences without supporting experiments.

Q02 and Q10 were weak for a different reason: no quench experiment had been performed. I assigned a small selectivity-preservation benefit to quenching, while acknowledging broad overlap. Even that point-direction was conjectural. A quench might have no effect after the completed heat operation, might add thermal or mixing risk, or might change degradation in a way not represented by the source data.

All blind batches changed the catalyst-to-reagent ratio, concentrations, total scale, and stirring relative to the source campaign. The prediction rationale introduced a 1.3 rate multiplier for the larger catalyst ratio, but no catalyst-order or concentration experiment justified that multiplier. Therefore the conversion intervals for Q01, Q03, Q05, Q09, and Q11 were probably too narrow. The very high conversion point estimates also compressed uncertainty near the upper bound.

This is partly inconsistent with K1's limitations. K1 explicitly restricted the empirical equations to catalyst B in acetonitrile, about 330–370 K, and up to roughly 7200 s, and stated that catalyst-dose effects were unidentified. Most blind queries were outside the temperature range and all used a changed formulation. The prediction text acknowledged the extrapolation, but some numerical intervals conveyed more confidence than those K1 warnings warranted. Q11 was thermally closest to the studied domain, yet even it inherited unmeasured catalyst-loading and concentration effects.

7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

The sealed recommendation selected batch-0009: catalyst B in water near 350 K for 3600 s. It was justified by an observed yield of about 0.288, selectivity of 0.671, lower degradation warning, and substantially lower risk than the matched organic-solvent batches. This was a defensible within-campaign choice, but it was not proof of a global optimum.

The recommendation has several limitations:

- It rests on one water batch with no exact replicate.
- Its small yield differences from ethanol, acetonitrile, and toluene are comparable to the level at which process and assay variability matter. The recommendation depends mainly on the larger selectivity and risk advantages, not on a proven yield advantage.
- Only one temperature, time, and catalyst loading were tested in water.
- Catalyst B was not compared with catalysts A, C, and D in water, so the catalyst-by-solvent interaction is unknown.
- No quench policy was tested.
- The selected condition was the best observed balanced safe condition, not necessarily the sample with maximum yield; batch-0006 had higher measured yield.

Repeatability should first be tested with several exact independent replicates of batch-0009, using both midpoint HPLC and final assay. Local robustness should then be assessed with small perturbations around 350 K and 3600 s, together with catalyst-loading and stirring perturbations. A compact local design such as 340/350/360 K and 3000/3600/4200 s would reveal whether the recommendation lies on a broad plateau or a narrow ridge.

Cross-material robustness requires testing at least catalyst C in water because C showed a potentially useful selectivity/activity tradeoff in acetonitrile. Testing water against one nearby solvent formulation under replicated conditions would establish whether the observed branching advantage is robust rather than a single categorical coincidence.

Cross-world generalization is much weaker. The catalysts and reaction species are anonymous latent benchmark entities, and the public material information expressly disallows interpreting categorical solvent effects as universal real-solvent chemistry. Consequently, batch-0009 is only a within-world recommendation. It should not be presented as a transferable chemical recipe without an independent calibration campaign in the new world.

In short, batch-0009 was the highest observed balanced operating choice in this finite sample. It was not replicated, not locally optimized, not proven robust to formulation changes, and not demonstrated to be globally optimal.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 9 used catalyst B in water near 350 K for 3600 s and retained about 0.288 yield with substantially higher selectivity and lower safety risk than the matched organic-solvent conditions, providing the best balanced safe operating point.
